say.text: Your registrar says: 'For the psoas sign you flex the right hip and rotate it inwards.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: You're right: flexed internal rotation is the psoas test
Psoas needs hip extension; flexed internal rotation is obturator
Psoas extension points to a pelvic appendix, which lies in the pelvis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Extending the right hip stretches the psoas. Flexing it and rotating it inwards tenses the obturator internus.
A retrocaecal appendix lies on the psoas, so the psoas sign points to a retrocaecal tip, the commonest position (K92).
Tempting: both are right-hip manoeuvres that hurt in the same lower abdomen, so the names feel swappable.
But flexing and rotating the hip inwards tests the obturator, not the psoas. The psoas sign needs the hip extended (K38, K39).
What is right: psoas is extension; obturator is flexion with internal rotation. The movement sets the name (K106).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the movement first: extension is psoas, internal rotation of the flexed hip is obturator.

say.text: Tempting: the psoas sign is a hip test, and the hip is close to the pelvis, so the pelvic position feels like a neighbour.
But the psoas sign suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas. The pelvic position goes with the obturator sign (K38, K39).
What is right: pair each sign with the muscle it stresses, and the muscle with the position it touches (K93).

sure_note.text: You were sure the psoas sign means pelvic. Psoas means retrocaecal; obturator means pelvic (K38, K39).

say.text: Ask which muscle each movement stretches or tenses. Then ask which part of the caecum or pelvis lies against that muscle.
You want Rovsing's sign, and the patient's pain is in the right iliac fossa.
Where do you press?

choices.label: Right iliac fossa, where the pain is

say.text: Yes. Pressure in the left iliac fossa pushes gas towards the caecum, and the inflamed right iliac fossa hurts (K37).
So Rovsing's sign is pressure on one side and pain on the other. The pain is never on the side you press (K106).
Tempting: the sign seems to be named for where the pain is, so you press where the patient hurts.
But pressing the inflamed side tests the local tenderness, not Rovsing's mechanism. The sign needs pressure away from the pain (K37).
What is right: press the left iliac fossa, and the pain felt in the right iliac fossa is Rovsing's sign (K37, K106).

sure_note.text: You were sure you press where it hurts. Rovsing is pressure on the left, pain on the right (K37).

say.text: A student lists the early course of a typical case of appendicitis.
Which order is right?

choices.label: Right iliac fossa pain first, then pain at the umbilicus
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Pain comes first, then anorexia and vomiting, and fever later (K6, K31).
Vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis, so the order is itself the discriminator (K6).
Tempting: vomiting is the first symptom in gastroenteritis and in obstruction, so it feels like an opening symptom here.
But in typical appendicitis vomiting follows the pain. Vomiting first argues against the diagnosis (K6, K31).
What is right: pain, then vomiting, then fever. The order carries the diagnosis (K6).

sure_note.text: You were sure vomiting comes first. In appendicitis it follows pain, and that order is the clue (K6).

say.text: Tempting: the pain ends in the right iliac fossa, so the student has started from where it finally settles.
But early pain is visceral and periumbilical, from the T10 supply. It reaches the right iliac fossa only when the parietal peritoneum is involved (K26, K27).
What is right: pain begins periumbilical and shifts to the right iliac fossa later (K5, K30).

sure_note.text: You were sure the right iliac fossa pain comes first. The migration runs from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa (K30).

say.text: Ask which pain is visceral and comes from the midgut supply, and which pain needs the parietal peritoneum to be involved.
A patient has rebound tenderness, right iliac fossa tenderness, leucocytosis, anorexia, nausea, fever and a left shift. He has no migration of pain.
What is his Alvarado total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each; rebound, anorexia, nausea, fever and left shift score 1 each (K7, K107).
Two 2-point items and five 1-point items give 9. A total of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely (K47).
Tempting: rebound tenderness is a peritoneal sign, so it feels as if it deserves the top weight with tenderness.
But only right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2. Rebound scores 1, so 10 overcounts (K107, K7).
What is right: two 2-point items and five 1-point items total 9. Count the weights in the table (K7).

sure_note.text: You were sure rebound scores 2. The table gives it 1; only tenderness and leucocytosis take 2 (K107).

say.text: Tempting: a left shift is a fine detail of the blood film, so it feels too small to count.
But left shift is a 1-point item of its own. Leaving it out understates the score (K7).
What is right: 2 + 2 for the two 2-point items, then 1 for each of the five others, total 9 (K7, K107).

sure_note.text: You were sure left shift scores nothing. Every other item in the score scores 1 (K7).

say.text: Score in pairs: which two items carry 2 points, and what does every other item carry?
A house officer says: 'Ultrasound is the investigation of choice in every adult, so a negative scan ends the work-up.'
Which reply is right?

choices.label: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice at every age
A negative scan in an adult is decisive; discharge
CT is most accurate in adults; a negative scan doesn't exclude it

say.text: Yes. CT is the most accurate test in adults, and ultrasound is first only in children and pregnancy (K99, K98).
A negative ultrasound in an adult does not close the question, so the work-up goes on to CT (K55).
Tempting: ultrasound is the test named in most past-paper stems, so it feels like the answer for everyone.
But the old key expected ultrasound as the investigation of choice in general (K108). That key does not describe adults, where CT is the most accurate test (K99).
What is right: teach both. PYQs expected ultrasound in general; current practice uses it first in children and pregnancy, and CT for adults (K98).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age: the ultrasound key fits children and pregnancy, not adults (K98).

say.text: Tempting: a scan that shows nothing feels reassuring, and the ultrasound is the test you ordered.
But in an adult a negative ultrasound does not exclude appendicitis. CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity (K55).
What is right: a negative ultrasound in an adult leads to contrast CT, not to discharge (K55, K99).

sure_note.text: You were sure a negative scan is decisive in an adult. It is not; CT is the test that settles it (K55).

say.text: A 9-year-old boy and a 31-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks both have right iliac fossa pain.
Which first imaging is right for each?

choices.label: Contrast CT for both, since CT is the most accurate test
Ultrasound for the boy, MRI for the woman

say.text: Yes. Ultrasound is the first test in children and in pregnancy, as graded compression (K98, K54).
Pregnancy keeps the same first rung. MRI is added only if ultrasound is inconclusive (K56).
Tempting: CT is the most accurate test, so it feels like the safest choice for any patient with right iliac fossa pain.
But accuracy is not the first question. Children and pregnant women get ultrasound first; CT is the adult test (K98, K99).
What is right: ultrasound first for both the boy and the pregnant woman (K98).

sure_note.text: You were sure CT is right. Children and pregnant women start with ultrasound, whatever the accuracy (K98).

say.text: Tempting: MRI avoids radiation and is very accurate, so it feels like the best first test in pregnancy.
But MRI is the second rung, used when ultrasound is inconclusive, not the first (K56, K100).
What is right: ultrasound first for the pregnant woman and for the boy; MRI only if ultrasound fails (K98, K100).

sure_note.text: You were sure MRI comes first in pregnancy. The first rung is ultrasound; MRI follows an inconclusive scan (K100).

say.text: A 22-year-old woman has right iliac fossa pain and nausea. Her last period was seven weeks ago. The house surgeon wants her in theatre.
What do you do first?

choices.label: Contrast CT now; the pregnancy test can follow
Appendicectomy now; right iliac fossa pain in a woman is appendicitis
Serum or urine beta-hCG before any scan or theatre

say.text: Yes. Every woman of reproductive age needs a beta-hCG, because ectopic pregnancy changes the imaging and the operation (K53, K59).
Right iliac fossa pain in a woman has several causes, so the test comes before the label (K59).
Tempting: the appendix is the likely cause, so imaging it now feels like the efficient step.
But a scan before beta-hCG can miss an ectopic pregnancy, which changes the whole plan (K53, K59).
What is right: beta-hCG first, then imaging or surgery as the findings direct (K53).

sure_note.text: You were sure imaging comes first. The pregnancy test changes everything, so it goes first (K53).

say.text: Tempting: right iliac fossa pain with nausea looks like the textbook picture, so surgery feels like the logical next step.
But right iliac fossa pain is not always appendicitis. In women, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cysts and pelvic inflammatory disease share it (K59).
What is right: beta-hCG first; then choose imaging or theatre for the likeliest cause (K53, K59).

sure_note.text: You were sure this pain means appendicitis. In women it has gynaecological causes too (K59).

say.text: Two adults have CT-proven appendicitis. Patient A has uncomplicated disease with no appendicolith. Patient B is the same but has an appendicolith.
Which patient is a candidate for antibiotics-first?

choices.label: Patient B, since antibiotics-first now applies to every CT-proven case
Patient A, the one without an appendicolith
Neither: appendicectomy is the only treatment for both

say.text: Yes. Antibiotics-first is accepted for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease (K71).
An appendicolith predicts failure and a higher perforation risk, so it moves the patient to surgery (K15, K71).
Tempting: CT has confirmed appendicitis, and antibiotics-first is now mentioned as an option, so the label feels like it fits.
But the appendicolith is an exclusion. It predicts antibiotic failure, so it takes the patient off the non-operative pathway (K71, K15).
What is right: antibiotics-first suits uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith, which is Patient A (K12, K71).

sure_note.text: You were sure Patient B qualifies. The appendicolith is the qualifier that excludes antibiotics-first (K71).

say.text: Tempting: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice in every past-paper answer, so 'only' feels fair.
But treatment of choice is not the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults (K110, K9).
What is right: appendicectomy stays the default; antibiotics-first is an option for selected patients (K9, K110).

sure_note.text: You were sure appendicectomy is the only option. The old key said so, but current practice accepts antibiotics-first in selected patients (K110).

say.text: A 58-year-old man's appendicular mass has resolved on the regimen.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Routine interval appendicectomy at six to eight weeks
Colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma, then decide on surgery
Immediate appendicectomy, since the mass proves the appendix is diseased

say.text: Yes. Interval surgery is now selective, and an older patient needs colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma (K75).
Decide on surgery after the work-up, not from the calendar (K75).
Tempting: interval appendicectomy at six to eight weeks is the classic answer, so it feels like the routine.
But that was the PYQ expectation. Current practice makes interval surgery selective and checks older patients first (K109, K75).
What is right: for a 58-year-old, exclude caecal carcinoma first, then decide on surgery (K75).

sure_note.text: You were sure the calendar decides. The routine is now selective, with work-up in older patients (K109).

say.text: Tempting: the mass proves the appendix is diseased, so removing it now feels like the logical step.
But the mass has resolved on the regimen, so immediate surgery is not indicated. Surgery follows a failing regimen (K73, K74).
What is right: work-up for caecal carcinoma first, then a selective decision on interval surgery (K75).

sure_note.text: You were sure a mass means immediate surgery. A resolved mass is managed by work-up and selection (K75).

say.text: A 45-year-old man with appendicitis develops rigors, jaundice and liver abscesses.
Which complication is this?

choices.label: Pylephlebitis, septic thrombosis of the portal vein

say.text: Yes. Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system, with rigors, jaundice and liver abscesses (K80).
It is a complication of the disease itself, so it is not a problem of the operation (K80, K78).
Tempting: once the appendix is out, the fistula is the complication everyone remembers, so it feels like the episode's complication.
But a faecal fistula comes from a slipped stump or caecal necrosis after surgery. It is an operative complication (K84).
What is right: rigors, jaundice and liver abscesses point to the portal vein, which is pylephlebitis (K80).

sure_note.text: You were sure the fistula fits. A fistula is an operative complication from the stump (K84).

say.text: Tempting: wound infection is the most common complication after appendicectomy, so it feels like the default answer.
But it is the commonest operative complication, not a disease complication, and it does not explain rigors and jaundice (K82).
What is right: pylephlebitis, septic portal thrombophlebitis with liver abscesses (K80).

sure_note.text: You were sure wound infection fits. It is the commonest operative complication, not the cause of rigors and jaundice (K82).

say.text: The gridiron incision splits the oblique muscles along their fibres. A nerve in its path, if cut, gives a right inguinal hernia.
Which nerve is it?
Yes. The ilioinguinal nerve is injured with a gridiron incision, and the injury gives a right inguinal hernia (K85).
The gridiron splits the muscles along their fibres, so the nerve in the path is the one at risk (K65).
Tempting: the iliac-region nerves are learned together as one bundle, so a neighbour feels equally likely.
But the gridiron path, not the bundle, decides which nerve is at risk. The iliohypogastric is a neighbour, not the nerve that gives this hernia (K65).
What is right: the ilioinguinal nerve, injured with a gridiron incision, gives a right inguinal hernia (K85).

sure_note.text: You were sure the neighbour is the one. The nerve is the ilioinguinal, which the gridiron crosses (K85).

say.text: Tempting: the genitofemoral nerve runs close to the inguinal canal, so it feels like the nerve at risk.
But running near the canal is not the same as being the nerve the gridiron crosses to produce this hernia (K65, K85).
What is right: the ilioinguinal nerve is injured with a gridiron incision, giving a right inguinal hernia (K85).

sure_note.text: You were sure the genitofemoral is at risk. The hernia comes from the ilioinguinal nerve (K85).

say.text: Acute appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen. Which is the commonest tumour of the appendix itself?

choices.label: Adenocarcinoma, since it is the most serious

say.text: Yes. Carcinoid, the neuroendocrine tumour, is the commonest appendix tumour and usually sits at the tip (K105, K89).
PYQs expected under 2 cm at the tip to need appendicectomy alone, and over 2 cm to need right hemicolectomy (K111).
Keep the two commonest facts apart: appendicitis for the emergency, carcinoid for the tumour (K1, K105).
Tempting: a mucocele is a familiar appendix lesion, and its name sounds like the answer for a frequent finding.
But a mucocele can rupture and cause pseudomyxoma peritonei. It is a complication to recognise, not the commonest tumour (K90).
What is right: carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour, usually at the tip (K105).

sure_note.text: You were sure a mucocele is the commonest. The commonest is carcinoid; the mucocele is a risk of rupture (K90).

say.text: Tempting: the tumour that sounds most serious feels like the one an exam would call most common.
But severity and frequency are different questions. Carcinoid, not adenocarcinoma, is the commonest appendix tumour (K105).
What is right: carcinoid, usually at the tip, is the commonest; the size rule then decides surgery (K105, K111).

sure_note.text: You were sure the most serious-sounding tumour is the commonest. Frequency and severity are separate (K105).
